# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature during selective coronary angiography, in the absence of significant obstructive epicardial disease. The coronary slow flow phenomenon is an angiographic finding characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease. [1] It was first described more than five decades ago: A A Tambe, M A Demany, H A Zimmerman and E Mascarenhas reported it in the American Heart Journal in 1972. [2] Since then, the condition has acquired several synonyms, including coronary slow flow syndrome, cardiac syndrome Y, and primary coronary slow flow. Coronary slow flow phenomenon, also known as cardiac syndrome Y, is defined as the delayed opacification of the coronary vasculature at the distal level. [3]

It is important to distinguish primary CSFP from secondary causes of slow flow. "Primary" CSFP should be distinguished from delayed contrast progression in the context of reperfusion therapy such as angioplasty or stenting for acute myocardial infarction, or other "secondary" causes that include coronary artery ectasia, coronary artery spasm, valvular heart disease, or connective tissue disorders. [4]

## Quantification

The principal quantitative tool is the corrected TIMI frame count (CTFC), introduced by Gibson and colleagues. Although the TIMI flow grade is a valuable and widely used qualitative measure, it is limited by its subjective and categorical nature; the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardized distal landmarks was therefore counted to objectively assess an index of coronary blood flow as a continuous variable. [5] Because the left anterior descending artery is longer than the other vessels, its frame count is divided by 1.7. The LAD frame counts are divided by 1.7 to correct for the longer length, with all films corrected at 30 frames per second; a CTFC above 27 frames in at least one major vessel defines CSFP. [6] More recent guideline statements have incorporated this threshold as evidence of microvascular impairment. Coronary Vasomotion Disorders International Study recommendations recognize coronary slow flow phenomenon (defined as corrected TFC > 27) as evidence of impaired microvascular dysfunction. [7]

## Epidemiology and Clinical Presentation

CSFP is not rare. It has clinical implications such as angina, acute coronary syndrome and sudden death, with a prevalence ranging from 1–5% of coronary angiograms and is more frequent in young male smokers. [3] A large prospective series confirmed these associations. CSFP was identified in 5.5% of subjects referred for angiography, who were more obese and had lower high-density lipoprotein levels; the condition was associated with male sex and obesity. [8] Hypertension features prominently among predictors. Among 3600 patients scheduled for angiography, 2% met slow-flow criteria, and multivariable analysis identified low body mass index, hypertension, low HDL cholesterol and high hemoglobin as independent predictors, with hypertension the strongest. [9] Recurrent angina dominates the clinical picture, and over 80% of patients experience recurrent chest pain, resulting in considerable impairment in quality of life. [10] Importantly, CSFP can also manifest acutely, as in non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction with reversibility on intracoronary adenosine. An intracoronary adenosine challenge showed normalization of the TIMI frame count, and the patient was given the diagnosis of coronary slow flow and started on amlodipine. [11]

## Pathophysiology

CSFP is best conceptualized as a primarily microvascular disorder, although its mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Histopathological work first implicated the small vessels. In patients with angina but angiographically patent major arteries, significantly reduced contrast flow velocity was documented compared with controls. [12] Subsequent biopsy studies described fibromuscular hyperplasia, medial hypertrophy, myointimal proliferation, as well as endothelial edema, thickening and degeneration in the coronary microvessels. [10] Resting microvascular resistance is characteristically elevated. Invasive studies have demonstrated that resting coronary artery resistances are abnormally elevated in these patients, in contrast with classic syndrome X, where these resistances respond normally to vasodilator stimuli. [13]

Hemodynamic and metabolic studies support transient ischemia. The Beltrame group performed coronary sinus studies demonstrating coronary hemodynamic findings at rest and during provocative stimuli, with biochemical evidence of inducible myocardial ischemia. [14] Endothelial dysfunction is a recurring theme. Endothelin-1 and nitric oxide concentrations were assessed before and at the peak of exercise testing, with a mean TIMI frame count in patients of 54.1. [15] Reduced nitric-oxide–generating capacity has been corroborated: endothelial dysfunction plays a key role in the aetiopathogenesis of slow coronary flow even without obstructive lesions, and reduced plasma levels of endothelial nitric oxide synthase are an important indicator of this dysfunction. [16] Microvascular spasm may be a mechanistic contributor: coronary microvascular spasm can be the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of the slow coronary flow phenomenon, with coronary flow highly dependent on microvascular resistance, which is increased during spasm. [17]

Diffuse, non-obstructive atherosclerosis also contributes. Using IVUS, investigators demonstrated diffuse intimal thickening, widespread calcification, and non-obstructive atheromatous changes, providing evidence that CSFP may reflect diffuse, non-obstructive atherosclerotic disease together with microvascular disease. [18] Inflammatory and oxidative pathways are implicated, including thioredoxin-interacting protein–mediated injury. Plasma TXNIP and malondialdehyde levels are increased in patients with slow coronary flow, and deletion of endothelial TXNIP increases nitric oxide production while lessening oxidative stress and endothelial inflammation. [19] Genetic susceptibility has been explored. In a study of 180 patients with CSFP and 87 controls, the allelic distribution of eNOS 894G/T was significantly associated with CSFP. [20] Broader work links endothelial dysfunction with inflammatory mediators such as CRP, which down-regulates endothelial nitric oxide synthase transcription and destabilizes eNOS mRNA, resulting in decreased nitric oxide. [21] CSFP overlaps conceptually with the broader spectrum of microvascular angina. CSFP is increasingly recognized as a separate clinical entity alongside classic syndrome X because the two differ mechanistically, have differing clinical features, and CSFP's prognosis is not as benign as traditionally described. [13]

## Prognosis

Although mortality is low, CSFP is not entirely benign. In a cohort followed for a mean of 3.8 years, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 39 of 421 patients (9.3%). [22] Risk was independently associated with age over 50 years, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. [22] In acute settings, CSFP carries prognostic weight: CSFP was an independent predictor of MACE (adjusted HR 2.76) and is associated with a higher risk of adverse events among patients with MINOCA. [23] Life-threatening arrhythmias have been reported. Presentations of CSF often include life-threatening conditions such as acute coronary syndrome, cerebrovascular events, and severe arrhythmias including ventricular fibrillation. [24]

## Management

No definitive disease-modifying therapy exists, and treatment is largely empirical and symptom-directed. Various medications have been evaluated for the treatment of CSFP; however, the actual efficacies of the majority of these pharmacological agents have not been established. [25] Calcium-channel blockade is a mainstay. Intracoronary nifedipine eliminates the angiographic findings of CSFP, and calcium blockade is effective in reducing and improving symptoms. [25] The best randomized evidence comes from the T-channel blocker mibefradil: without changing epicardial vessel diameter or rate–pressure product, mibefradil improved TIMI frame count in vessels exhibiting TIMI-2 flow and, compared with placebo, reduced total angina frequency by 56% and prolonged episodes by 74%. [26] (Mibefradil was subsequently withdrawn for drug-interaction reasons but remains a proof-of-concept.) Statins may help via anti-inflammatory and endothelial effects: simvastatin may improve myocardial perfusion abnormality in slow coronary flow, and atorvastatin improves coronary flow and endothelial function in patients with coronary slow flow. [27,28] Nebivolol, with its nitric-oxide–mediated vasodilatory properties, has shown benefit on endothelial function. Nebivolol improves flow-mediated dilation in patients with slow coronary flow, with reported symptom improvement in 90% of patients. [29] Finally, a dual-acting vasodilator outperformed nitrate monotherapy: patients treated with nicorandil had fewer angina episodes than those on nitroglycerin, and nicorandil provided better symptomatic relief of angina than nitroglycerin. [30]

## Conclusion

CSFP is a clinically relevant, mechanistically heterogeneous disorder reflecting microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, subclinical atherosclerosis, and inflammation. It causes substantial morbidity through recurrent angina and is associated with adverse outcomes that are not negligible. Quantification by CTFC enables reproducible diagnosis, but therapy remains empirical; calcium-channel blockers, statins, nebivolol, and nicorandil offer symptomatic benefit. Further mechanistic and randomized work is needed to define optimal management.
